title: Atoms and the Periodic Table
seo_title: Grade 9 Science (SNC1W): Atoms and the Periodic Table Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: How experimental evidence led to new atomic models; the location, relative mass and charge of protons, neutrons and electrons in the Bohr–Rutherford model; the link between an element's position in the periodic table and its atomic structure; and the properties of elements and periodic trends. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Science, Grade 9: SNC1W (2022), Strand C: Nature of Matter)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Science (SNC1W) worksheets on atoms and the periodic table: atomic models, protons, neutrons and electrons, Bohr–Rutherford diagrams, groups and periods, and families of elements. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Protons = atomic number; electrons = protons in a neutral atom.
body_html:
How to think about it

Atomic models changed as new evidence appeared: Dalton (solid spheres), Thomson (electrons in a positive sphere), Rutherford (a tiny dense nucleus) and Bohr (electrons in shells). Protons (+1) and neutrons (0) are in the nucleus and have about the same mass; electrons (−1) are about 1/1836 of that mass and move around the nucleus.

The atomic number is the number of protons. In a Bohr–Rutherford diagram, shells hold 2, 8, 8 electrons. Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons and similar properties; the period (row) number is the number of occupied shells.

Example

Sodium-23 (Z = 11). Protons, neutrons, electrons?

p = 11, e = 11

n = 23 − 11 = 12

Answer: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons

Example

Draw the shells of magnesium (Z = 12).

2 in the first shell, 8 in the second

2 left for the third

Answer: 2, 8, 2

Common mistakes

  • Using the mass number as the number of protons.
  • Putting 8 electrons in the first shell.
  • Thinking elements in the same period have similar properties: groups do.

faq.q: What did Rutherford's gold-foil experiment show?
faq.a: Most alpha particles passed through, but a few bounced back, so an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space.
Their outer shells are full, so they do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.

items.e: The model of the atom changed as new evidence was found.

items.q: What is the relative mass of a proton?
items.e: Protons and neutrons have relative mass 1; an electron's is about 1/1840.

items.q: What is the charge on a proton?

items.q: What did J. J. Thomson contribute?
c: He arranged the elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements.
He described atoms as tiny solid spheres that cannot be divided.
He discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model.
He showed with the alpha scattering experiment that the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus.
items.e: Models change with evidence.

items.q: What did Ernest Rutherford contribute?
c: He described atoms as tiny solid spheres that cannot be divided.
He arranged the elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements.
He showed with the alpha scattering experiment that the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus.
items.e: Models change with evidence.

items.e: Valence electrons are in the outer shell.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of phosphorus (proton number 15)?
items.e: Fill the shells in order: 2 in the first, 8 in the second, 8 in the third. Phosphorus: 2, 8, 5.

items.q: What is the electron arrangement (shells) of a phosphorus atom (15 electrons)?

items.q: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a silicon atom (proton number 14)?

items.q: How many valence electrons does selenium (Se) have? (It is in group 16.)
items.e: Groups 1–2: same as the group number. Groups 13–18: subtract 10 (helium has 2).

items.e: Groups 1–2: same as the group number. Groups 13–18: subtract 10 (helium has 2).

items.q: Which is more reactive, potassium (K) or rubidium (Rb)?
items.e: Alkali metals get more reactive down the group (easier to lose 1 electron).

items.q: Which is more reactive with water: sodium or rubidium?
items.e: Reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the group: the outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily.

items.q: Which is more reactive: bromine or fluorine?
items.e: Reactivity of the halogens decreases down Group 17.

items.q: What is iodine like at room temperature?
items.e: Down Group 17 the colour darkens and the state changes from gas to liquid to solid.

items.q: Aqueous iodine is added to aqueous potassium bromide. What happens?
c: No reaction, because iodine is less reactive than bromine.
items.e: A less reactive halogen cannot displace a more reactive one.
